toc.title: What people have tried, and what helped most
Nine or more supports, and still stuck
What helped outside of professional support

blocks.p: So many people are stuck in shutdown, and each of them thinks they're alone. They each think they're different, or that they're hopeless. You might be one of those people. But it's not hopeless, and you're not alone. Your shutdown experiences are probably really similar to other people's in shutdown, and I can actually show you.

I sent out a shutdown experiences survey to my email list, and about 75 people responded. Real people, experiencing real shutdown. Here I want to focus on what they told me are their most helpful resources. I hope you feel validated and less alone after reading this, and a big, big thanks to everyone who took the time to complete the survey.

blocks.h: What people have tried, and what helped most

blocks.p: The first question was really two questions I'll look at together: which of these supports have you tried, and which was most helpful? The options were:

ul: Informative content, like articles and blogs
Interactive content, like workshops and webinars
Group support, like forums or support groups
Self-help tools, like apps and journals
Structured or guided substance use, like cannabis, MDMA, or ayahuasca

blocks.p: People could also fill in other things they'd tried, and they could pick as many as they had actually tried. It wasn't limited to one.

The highest was informative content: 86 percent of people said they'd tried it. That makes total sense. They probably found stuff on YouTube or Instagram, even the one-minute reel kind of things, plus books and blogs. I think that's usually the starting point. We learn before we put anything into practice.

58 percent of respondents said informative content was actually the most helpful. It's possible that people take in informative content and just stop there. I think that's really common. We learn, we learn, we learn, but we don't take action on it.

74 percent of respondents said they had tried therapy. My audience is not exactly a general audience. It's people who are actively looking for ways to improve their life or get unstuck, so three out of four people having tried therapy doesn't shock me. Of those 74 percent, about half said therapy was their most helpful support.

I've heard from many people in therapy who get some kind of benefit from it, or who don't get benefit and maybe even feel retraumatized. That's definitely within the realm of possibility. Then they find content like this that they find really helpful. They learn about the Polyvagal Theory and the shutdown state and how to recover, and that stuff isn't covered in their therapy. So it makes sense to me why more people would say informative content is the most helpful: it just makes sense to them. Maybe it's helpful because it normalizes them and validates their experiences. But knowing what to do with it is a different thing. And therapists, well, we're not all trained in this kind of somatic and Polyvagal Theory stuff.

At the lowest end, which I think is pretty predictable, were retreats at 13 percent and guided substance use at 21 percent. Both involve a hefty investment of time, of trust in another, and of money. It makes total sense that they'd be at the lower end.

blocks.h: Nine or more supports, and still stuck

blocks.p: What I found most interesting out of all of this is how many supports people had tried. The most common number was nine or 10. Almost a quarter, almost one in four people, had tried nine or 10 supports. That's a lot. It really struck me. On top of that, almost 41 percent of respondents had tried nine or more, and were still stuck in some noticeable amount of shutdown.

It also kind of makes sense. Shutdown's not easy, especially if we're not recognizing that it's shutdown. If someone is treating it as a chemical imbalance and just medicating, tweaking medications, doing more medication, or if their therapist is telling them, "You're depressed, this is forever, and you just have to manage it with more medication and coping skills," then not much is going to change. You might keep looking for the thing that's finally going to help.

Shutdown is not easy to come out of. It's probably the slowest, and it's the furthest down the [Polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system). Maybe that's one reason why. And when we're in shutdown, there's a lot of hopelessness. We feel empty. We feel alone. We don't believe in ourselves. So we keep trying the next thing, or relying on the next expert, and if we don't get results really quickly, we might give up and go to the next thing. But coming out of shutdown is a long process. It is obviously not quick, and it's not easy. There might be some patience lacking for that, and I don't blame anybody for that whatsoever.

On top of that, the signs of coming out of shutdown are increased flight or fight activation. There might be more irritation, frustration, or agitation. That's potentially a very good sign, as long as you're balancing it out with more and more safety activation. But it doesn't feel like a good sign. Someone might notice more agitation and think, "This isn't working. I'm doing the wrong thing." So they jump to the next technique or support, trying to fix it, or thinking that whatever they're doing is failing. But that returning mobilization is potentially a really good sign.

The next question was: how likely are you to ask for support? Only 9 percent of respondents were likely to ask for support. The vast majority, 91 percent, were unlikely to ask for support while in shutdown.

This makes sense. We feel very alone and very cut off, and isolation is often part of shutdown. In shutdown, the body needs to immobilize, and solitude might be a really good idea. Not isolation, where you're locking yourself away in a dark room. Solitude, where you go to a lake or a beach, take a walk around the block, or just sit in the backyard. Something where you're immobile and alone, but okay with it. Peaceful and relaxing, versus depressing and isolating.

Being alone is helpful. But having a couple of supports, people you trust and are close to, is not a bad idea at all. Connecting with others and receiving their co-regulation can help you come out of shutdown.
On that note, the next question was: do you have people in your life who can provide co-regulation? Over half said yes. The other half said no or maybe.

So half have people in their life who can provide co-regulation, but the vast majority are not willing to ask for it. And that makes sense. If you call someone up and say, "Hey, can you provide me with co-regulation?" it's probably not going to go well. You're probably going to feel weird doing it. But can you reconnect with someone in your life? Can you meet someone for lunch? Can you just call to hear their voice and say, "Hey, I just want to check in with you and see how you're doing," or "I miss you"? I think that's possible.

The next question was: how likely are you to receive co-regulation from a safe other? About 25 percent said they're likely to receive it. That's good, but it leaves 75 percent who will not, or might, receive co-regulation from a safe other.

So more people can receive co-regulation than ask for it, and that actually makes a lot of sense. No matter what defensive state we're in, we can usually receive some co-regulation, whether we're aware of it or not. Asking for it, putting yourself out there, risking vulnerability: that's a much taller order.
Deb Dana said something similar when I interviewed her:

q: In the beginning, for many people, climbing out of dorsal is really difficult... They need a co-regulator. They need somebody to accompany them.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana Interview: Story Follows State, Climbing the Ladder and Diagnosing (episode 29)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c)

blocks.h: What helped outside of professional support

blocks.p: Next I asked what experiences people have had with non-professional supports. I got a lot of responses, so here's a summary:

ul: Many found support from friends, partners, or peers helpful, especially those who understand trauma and co-regulation. If you know someone with this knowledge, that's going to be more helpful. How many of us have that? In this audience, maybe more than in the general population.
Some prefer handling their shutdown on their own first, through activities like movement, dance, or yoga, before reaching out to others.
Resources like books, courses, and online communities provide valuable insights. That top-down learning helps them manage their defensive activation or their shutdown.

Romantic partners can offer comfort, but their responses can either help or make things worse, depending on the partner's stability. Someone with a lot of access to their safety state, who can co-regulate, is obviously going to be more comforting than someone who can't.

blocks.p: Handling it on your own first makes total sense, and I think it's a really good idea. Receiving co-regulation from others is great, but having solitude might be the first step. Again, solitude is not isolation. Isolation is a dark room, cutting out the world, binging on your phone. Solitude is: I'm going to be by myself and give myself permission to feel all my feelings, whatever comes up in the present moment, and then dance, or journal about it, or do some yoga and stretch out. Or I'm going to go somewhere safe, like a beach if you have access to one, and just sit and be and think and feel.
Here's what four people shared, in their own words.
Someone who's been in shutdown for 11 to 30 years:

q: One of my best resources now is a couple of friends who are doing this work as well. We support each other and create the safe space and offer co-regulation. So powerful.

blocks.p: Someone who's been in shutdown for three to six months: "A bit of online yoga." Short and to the point.
Someone who's been in shutdown for 31 to 40 years:

q: Meditation techniques, for example, RAIN... The hardest thing is remembering/thinking to use them in the moment.

blocks.p: Absolutely. Learning these things is great, and I think there's some top-down benefit. But you have to implement it. You have to practice this stuff. I really encourage people to practice before the problem. Don't wait until you're at a seven out of 10 shutdown. Practice when you're at a two or three out of 10, or when you have more safety than not. Be mindful, and use the skills you're learning before you need them. Then when you need them, they'll be more accessible.
And someone who's been in shutdown within the past year:

q: The content and helping me understand why I am like this reduces my shame very significantly.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.p: Then I asked about experiences with professional supports. Here's the summary:

ul: Some people found professional help effective, especially somatic-based therapies and holistic approaches, particularly when they focused on co-regulation, touch, and attunement. I think the touch aspect is kind of interesting. A couple of people said that.
Several people shared that traditional talk therapy partially helped, but they felt like something was missing.

A few people said therapy worsened their experience or left them feeling misunderstood or even blamed. They emphasized that finding the right therapist, or maybe the right approach, is really important.
A couple of people preferred coaching over therapy, when the coaching was focused on change and education: goals and present-moment stuff.

Some people said they have never allowed professionals to witness their full shutdown state. They keep it in check, or hold it back, and of course that leads to them feeling like it was never addressed or recognized.

blocks.p: As long as you have a safe other, co-regulation is obviously going to be more helpful than not. And somatic mindfulness, being aware of your body, is going to be more helpful than thinking you have some sort of illness or disease, or that you have to get rid of your feelings. If you can be aware of them compassionately, that can actually help them soften and alleviate. For the people who felt like something was missing from talk therapy, I personally think the somatic piece is what's missing.

I would argue the right therapist is more important than the right approach. Even if you found someone who was Polyvagal informed and really good with somatic stuff, that doesn't mean they're a good fit for you. I think the techniques only go as far as the relationship does, but a balance of both would be ideal.

For people who hold their shutdown back, part of this is how much you bring to the table, what you share. But the therapist, or maybe coach, should also be able to recognize some of the experiences of shutdown if they're informed in this stuff. If not, it just looks like depression, and they'll say it's a chemical imbalance and you have to cope with it for the rest of your life.
Here's what two people shared about professional support. Someone who's been in shutdown for up to 50 years:

q: Spiritual psychotherapy has been my guiding star, as has been pranic healing/energy work to literally shift my energy when I cannot.

blocks.p: And someone in shutdown for up to 30 years:

q: For about seven years I have had therapy once a week. My therapy is somatic experiencing. And I still laughed at myself because I started with my therapist before I knew any of this stuff. But somatic experiencing and polyvagal kind of go hand in hand. So it works out very well for me. I have found my therapy to be very helpful. I am a huge proponent of coaching, but personally, I think I need more supports or have needed more intense support than what a coach could offer. I am also very limited on time, but if I didn't have therapy, I would certainly do coaching because I think that would be so beneficial and supportive for my growth and recovery.

blocks.p: I'm really happy for her. She found something that works for her, and it sounds like it aligns with what she needs. And I agree: somatic experiencing and the Polyvagal Theory definitely go hand in hand. I also agree that coaching is helpful, but you might need more support than that. Coaching is good for present-moment, goal-oriented work. Crises and more serious mental health stuff are obviously not a coaching thing, so therapy and more intensive supports could be totally appropriate for someone. Coaching is great for the person who's ready to change, who's just sick of it and ready to put something into action. I like how direct it is: we're here to make steps forward. As long as you have someone who's aligned with that, I think coaching can be really effective. I find it really enjoyable personally.

Thank you so much to everyone who shared their experiences of shutdown. A lot of people are stuck in shutdown, and there's also a lot of support for them. It's kind of cool to see the love and support for people, and the shared experiences of shutdown. I know there are people reading this and benefiting from it, so thank you to everyone who filled this out.
